newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: U.N. Council still in dispute on Haiti peacekeepers.
newsitem.headline: U.N. Council still in dispute on Haiti peacekeepers.

text.p: Russia is insisting the U.N. military mission in Haiti shut down in mid-1997, a position preventing the Security Council from taking a quick decision on extending the force on Friday, diplomats said.

Most council members, including Russia, have accepted a recommendation from Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali that the 1,300 troops and 286 civilian U.N. police stay in the Caribbean nation until June 30.
But Moscow wants the troops to go home by June, although it has no objections to keeping the international police in Haiti for seven months or longer, the diplomats said.
"Russia wants a clear plan two months before the end of the mandate on complete withdrawal of force," one envoy said.
The United States and Canada, which is heading the operation, apparently do not want to be tied down to assessing Haiti's future security needs at this time.

The mandate for the operation, known as the U.N. Support Mission in Haiti, expires on Friday. If no decision is reached by then, U.S. envoys suggested the council could approve a so-called "technical rollover" that would extend the force until Wednesday to allow further negotiations.
Despite concern among some leading Haitians about extending the foreign troops, President Rene Preval has asked for an eight month renewal as a minimum.
Russia has objected to so-called double-standards since the United Nations took over the operation from U.S. troops.

Its ambassador, Sergei Lavrov, has argued that the council has kept its missions small in turbulent Georgia and Tajikistan compared to a country of interest to Washington. Lavrov, however, has visited Haiti and agreed with the security concerns. Moscow has also fielded U.N. policemen.

The capability of the newly formed Haitian National Police force is at the centre of any decision on the peacekeepers. Dozens of police officers allegedly involved in crimes ranging from torture to theft have been purged and trainers say improvements have been made.

China too, which in June whittled down the number of troops and police currently in the country, has not agreed to the seven-month extension and advocated five months in its initial bargaining position.

Beijing has fought against the mission because of its anger at Haiti's ties with Taiwan, which it considers a renegade province. But relations have improved since a visit to Haiti in June by China's U.N. ambassador Qin Huasun

Last February, during the last renewal, China threatened to veto the military force in Haiti unless its numbers were reduced, prompting Canada to rescue the mission by paying for its own troops for six months.

Currently, the United Nations is paying for 600 troops, with the remaining 700 financed separately by Canada and the United States. Canada is fielding more than 700 troops while Pakistan has sent over 500.

One of the operation's main tasks is to train and monitor Haiti's fledgling police, which replaced the previous brutal paramilitary contingents loyal to the military junta that overthrew elected President Jean Bertrand Aristide in 1991.

He was restored to power three years later by a U.S.-led 22,000-member multinational force. The United Nations took over peacekeeping in March 1995 with 6,000 troops, a number reduced steadily since then.
